concepts.def: Hosts static sites (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images) built from a code repository. Files are served from points of presence around the world, and HTTPS certificates for custom domains are included.
concepts.ref: What is Azure Static Web Apps?

concepts.def: Managed hosting for web apps and APIs. You pick a plan tier and deploy code or a container; Azure runs, patches and load-balances the servers.

Azure runs the servers, operating system and patching; you bring code or files. You give up some control in exchange for much less operational work.

Prefer PaaS unless you need something only a virtual machine allows.
Traffic between users and your services travels over TLS (HTTPS), so nobody on the network path can read or change it. Most Azure PaaS services offer an HTTPS-only setting.
The Well-Architected pillar about spending only what the workload needs: right-size tiers, scale with demand and remove what you don't use.

Split an app into a presentation tier (the browser or phone), an application tier (your code) and a data tier (the database). Each tier talks only to its neighbour, so each can be secured and scaled on its own.
A managed relational database built on the SQL Server engine. Azure handles patching, backups and high availability; you choose a service tier (General Purpose, Business Critical or Hyperscale).

An identity in Microsoft Entra ID that Azure creates for a resource such as an App Service app. The app uses it to get tokens for other services, so there is no password or connection-string secret to store or rotate.
concepts.ref: What are managed identities for Azure resources?

concepts.def: Hosts DNS zones on Azure's global name servers. A public zone makes your domain resolve on the internet; a private zone resolves names only inside your virtual networks.

Free TLS certificates that App Service issues and renews for your custom domain. Together with the HTTPS-only setting, visitors always get an encrypted connection without you buying or rotating certificates.
concepts.ref: Add and manage TLS/SSL certificates in Azure App Service

concepts.def: Object storage for unstructured data such as images, video, documents and backups. Cheap per gigabyte, very durable, and readable over HTTPS from anywhere you allow.
Rough arithmetic with stated assumptions (users, requests, sizes) to size a design before building it. The goal is the right order of magnitude, not a precise number.
Give clients a short-lived, scoped token (a SAS) so they upload or download directly from storage instead of through your app. The app stays out of the data path and only hands out the key.
Keep session data out of the web servers (in a cache or database) so any instance can serve any request. Instances can then be added, removed or replaced without logging users out.
An in-memory data store used as a cache, session store or leaderboard. Reads take well under a millisecond. Formerly offered as Azure Cache for Redis.
Event-driven code that runs when a trigger fires: an HTTP request, a timer, a queue message, a new blob. On the Flex Consumption plan you pay for executions and it scales with the work.
APIs for sending email and SMS and for voice and video calling, so apps don't need a separate mail server or SMS gateway.

An external system calls an HTTPS endpoint you expose when something happens, such as a payment succeeding. The sender usually retries until it gets a success response, so the same event can arrive more than once.

An operation is idempotent when doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. Retries and at-least-once delivery are everywhere in the cloud, so handlers must recognise repeats (for example by an event id) and skip them.
Serverless containers: you bring an image, Azure runs and scales it on rules such as HTTP traffic, queue length or CPU, all the way down to zero replicas.
A service that runs no instances while idle and starts them when work arrives. It costs almost nothing at rest; the trade-off is a cold start on the first request.
concepts.ref: Set scaling rules in Azure Container Apps

concepts.def: Virtual machines give full control and full responsibility. App Service runs web apps with little effort. Container Apps runs containers serverlessly. AKS gives full Kubernetes and needs a platform team. Pick the most managed option that meets the requirements.
Microsoft's global HTTP entry point: anycast edge locations, TLS, caching, routing across regions and an optional web application firewall. It replaces the classic Azure CDN tiers.
Add more instances instead of a bigger machine. With at least two instances behind a load balancer, the app also survives one instance failing or being patched.
concepts.ref: Architecture strategies for designing a reliable scaling strategy

concepts.def: Read-only copies of a database that the primary keeps up to date asynchronously. Send reads to the replicas to take load off the primary; writes still go to the primary, and replicas can lag slightly behind.
concepts.ref: Read replicas in Azure Database for PostgreSQL

concepts.def: Managed PostgreSQL (flexible server): Azure runs the server, backups and optional zone-redundant high availability; you keep the open-source engine and its extensions.
concepts.ref: Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server overview

concepts.def: A globally distributed NoSQL database with single-digit-millisecond point reads, automatic indexing, a choice of five consistency levels, and throughput measured in request units.

The property Cosmos DB uses to spread items across physical partitions. A good key has many distinct values, spreads reads and writes evenly, and is part of most queries, so lookups go to one partition.
concepts.ref: Partitioning and horizontal scaling in Azure Cosmos DB

concepts.def: Cosmos DB's currency for throughput. Every operation costs RUs: a point read of a 1 KB item costs about 1 RU, writes and queries cost more. You provision RU/s, use autoscale, or pay per request with serverless.
concepts.ref: Request Units in Azure Cosmos DB

concepts.def: A Cosmos DB partition key with up to three levels, such as tenant → user. A huge tenant can spread over many physical partitions while queries for one tenant are still routed efficiently.
concepts.ref: Hierarchical partition keys in Azure Cosmos DB

concepts.def: Cosmos DB offers five levels, from strongest to weakest: strong, bounded staleness, session, consistent prefix and eventual. Stronger levels give fresher reads at the cost of latency, availability and throughput. Session (read your own writes) is the default.
concepts.ref: Consistency levels in Azure Cosmos DB

concepts.def: Many Azure SQL databases sharing one pool of compute. Each database can burst when it needs to, and you pay for the pool rather than for every database's peak. A good fit for many small tenant databases with uneven load.
concepts.ref: Elastic pools help you manage and scale multiple databases in Azure SQL Database

concepts.def: Serving many customers (tenants) from shared infrastructure. Designs range from a database per tenant to shared tables with a tenant id; each choice trades isolation against cost and operations.
A SQL Database tier built for very large databases: storage grows on its own up to about 128 TB, backups are near-instant snapshots, and read replicas can be added for read scale-out.
Fully managed file shares that speak SMB and NFS. Lift-and-shift apps that expect a network drive can mount them without code changes.

A network interface with a private IP address inside your virtual network that connects to a PaaS service over Private Link. With public network access turned off, the service is unreachable from the internet.

LRS keeps three copies in one data center; ZRS spreads them over three availability zones; GRS and GZRS add an asynchronous copy in a paired region. The RA- variants let you read the secondary copy while the primary region is down.

Hot, cool, cold and archive tiers trade storage price against access price and latency. Lifecycle management rules move blobs to cheaper tiers as they age. Archived blobs must be rehydrated (hours) before they can be read.
Time-based retention or legal-hold policies make blobs write-once, read-many: nobody, not even an administrator, can change or delete them until the policy allows it.
concepts.ref: Overview of immutable storage for blob data

concepts.def: Physically separate groups of data centers within one Azure region, each with independent power, cooling and networking. Zone-redundant services keep running when one zone fails.

The app looks in the cache first; on a miss it reads the database and writes the result into the cache with an expiry. Simple and resilient (the cache can be lost), but the first read is slow and data can be stale until it expires.
Every write goes to the cache and the database together, so the cache is always fresh. Reads never miss on recently written data, at the cost of slower writes and caching data that may never be read.

When a very popular key expires, thousands of requests miss at once and all hit the database. Defences: let one request refresh the key while others wait or get the stale value (a lock or early refresh), and add random jitter to TTLs so keys don't expire together.

What a full cache throws away. LRU evicts the least recently used keys; LFU evicts the least frequently used, which protects items that are always hot. noeviction refuses writes instead, which suits data stores, not caches.
concepts.ref: Memory management in Azure Managed Redis

concepts.def: Serving responses from points of presence near users instead of the origin. Static files and cacheable API responses come back in milliseconds, and the origin only sees cache misses.
Serve static files (scripts, styles, images, video) from storage through a CDN instead of from the web servers. The servers handle only dynamic requests, and files load from the edge.
An API gateway in front of your backends: subscription keys, JWT validation, rate limits, response caching, versioning and a developer portal, configured as policies instead of code.
Move shared concerns (TLS, authentication, rate limiting, caching) out of every service into the gateway. Services get simpler; the gateway becomes a critical component to run well.
Limit how many requests a caller can make in a period, and reject the rest with 429 Too Many Requests. It protects the backend from one noisy client and from sudden floods.
Running the app in two or more Azure regions behind a global entry point. Users get a nearby region and the app survives a regional outage, at the cost of data replication and more moving parts.

DNS-based traffic routing across endpoints and regions (priority, weighted, performance, geographic). It only answers DNS queries, so it works for any protocol but can't cache, terminate TLS or filter requests, and failover waits for DNS caches to expire.

Make the origin reachable only through the edge service, so attackers can't bypass the WAF and caching by calling the origin's address directly. With Front Door Premium, use a Private Link origin and turn off public access on the app.
concepts.ref: Secure traffic to Azure Front Door origins

concepts.def: Inspects HTTP requests and blocks common attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting. Microsoft-managed rule sets are updated for new threats; custom rules add rate limits and geo filters.
concepts.ref: What is Azure Web Application Firewall?

concepts.def: Adding and removing instances automatically based on metrics (CPU, requests, queue length) or a schedule. You pay for peak capacity only while the peak lasts.

A group of identical VMs managed as one: autoscale on metrics, rolling upgrades, and instances spread across availability zones. The usual way to run VM-based workloads that need more than one machine.
concepts.ref: What are Virtual Machine Scale Sets?

concepts.def: A layer 4 (TCP/UDP) load balancer. Standard SKU frontends can be zone-redundant; health probes take failed instances out of rotation. A cross-region (global) tier balances across regional load balancers.
A load balancer regularly checks each backend (a TCP connect or an HTTP path) and stops sending traffic to instances that fail. Without probes, a dead instance keeps receiving its share of requests.
A regional layer 7 (HTTP) load balancer inside your virtual network: TLS termination, path- and host-based routing, autoscaling and an optional WAF.

Layer 4 balancers forward TCP/UDP connections without looking inside, so they work for any protocol with minimal latency. Layer 7 balancers understand HTTP: they route by path or host, terminate TLS and filter requests, but only for web traffic.

Your private network in an Azure region, divided into subnets for different purposes. Resources in a VNet talk privately; only what you expose is reachable from outside. VNets and subnets span all availability zones of the region.
Allow and deny rules on traffic into and out of a subnet or network interface, by source, destination, port and protocol. The basic building block of network segmentation.
Browser-based RDP and SSH to VMs over TLS, from the Azure portal. VMs need no public IP and no open management ports to the internet.
Gives all outbound traffic from a subnet one or more static public IPs and a large pool of SNAT ports. Partners can allowlist one address, and busy apps stop running out of outbound ports.

A central hub VNet holds shared services (firewall, gateways, Bastion); each workload gets its own spoke VNet peered to the hub. Spokes route outbound traffic through the hub firewall, so one team inspects and controls it.
A managed, stateful network firewall with high availability built in. It filters traffic by network and application rules, and the Premium tier adds TLS inspection and intrusion detection.

A site-to-site VPN Gateway builds encrypted tunnels over the internet: quick and cheap, but with internet latency. ExpressRoute is a private circuit through a connectivity provider: predictable bandwidth and latency, at a higher cost and lead time.
concepts.ref: Connect an on-premises network to Azure

concepts.def: Several independent layers of protection (edge WAF, network segmentation, private endpoints, identity, encryption) so that one failed control doesn't expose the workload.

An enterprise message broker with queues (one consumer per message) and topics (a copy per subscription). It offers at-least-once delivery, dead-lettering, sessions for ordering, duplicate detection and scheduled messages.
Put a queue between the part that receives work and the part that does it. Bursts pile up in the queue instead of overwhelming the worker, and the caller gets an answer immediately.
The sender hands work to a broker and moves on, without waiting for the receiver. Services become independent in time and failure, at the cost of eventual consistency and harder debugging.
A publisher sends one message to a topic, and every interested subscriber gets its own copy. Adding a new consumer doesn't change the publisher.

A side queue where the broker moves messages that can't be processed, for example after too many delivery attempts. Poison messages stop blocking the main queue, and someone (or something) inspects and replays them.
concepts.ref: Overview of Service Bus dead-letter queues

concepts.def: Routes discrete events, such as "a blob was created" or "a resource changed", from Azure services or your own apps to handlers like Functions, queues and webhooks, with filtering and retries.
Producers emit events when something happens; consumers react independently. Systems become loosely coupled and react in near real time, but end-to-end flows are harder to follow.

Process related messages in order without giving up parallelism: messages carry a group key (a Service Bus session id), each group is handled in order by one consumer, and different groups run in parallel.
A partitioned, high-throughput event stream for telemetry and logs. Producers append events; each consumer group reads at its own pace, and Capture can write the raw stream to storage.

Service Bus can drop a message whose MessageId it has already seen within a time window. It catches resends by the sender, but not redeliveries to the consumer, so consumers still need to be idempotent.
Low-code workflows built from triggers and actions, with hundreds of connectors to SaaS apps and Azure services. Good for integration glue; less suited to heavy custom logic.
An extension of Azure Functions for stateful workflows written as code: orchestrators call activities, wait for events and timers, and survive restarts because their progress is checkpointed.
Start many tasks in parallel, then wait for all of them and combine the results. Durable Functions makes this a few lines of orchestrator code.
Store a large payload in storage and send only a reference (the claim check) in the message. Messages stay small and cheap, and only consumers that need the payload fetch it.
Sends push notifications to millions of devices through the phone platforms' push services, with tags for targeting and templates per platform.
Send urgent and routine work to separate queues (or with a priority) so urgent messages are processed first, even when routine work has piled up.
Several workers read from the same queue; each message goes to one of them. Throughput scales by adding workers, and a failed worker's messages go to the others.
The Well-Architected pillar about a workload doing what it should, when it should: redundancy, fault isolation, graceful degradation and recovery that has been tested.

Any component whose failure takes the whole workload down: one VM, one database without high availability, one gateway instance. Find them tier by tier and add redundancy where the business impact justifies the cost.
concepts.ref: Recommendations for performing failure mode analysis

concepts.def: When a request needs several services in a chain, their availabilities multiply: three 99.9% services in series give about 99.7%. Redundant, independent copies in parallel raise availability: 1 − (1 − A)².

Retry transient failures a few times, waiting longer each time (exponential backoff) with some randomness (jitter) so many clients don't retry in lockstep. Always pair retries with a timeout and a cap.

After repeated failures, stop calling a dependency for a while and fail fast (or use a fallback), then let a trial request through to see if it has recovered. It stops one slow dependency from tying up every caller.
When a non-essential dependency fails, keep the core working with reduced features, such as cached or default recommendations, instead of failing the whole page.
Isolate workloads into separate pools (compute, queues, connections) so one overloaded or failing part can't exhaust resources the others need, like the watertight compartments in a ship.

The recovery point objective (RPO) is how much data you can afford to lose, measured in time. The recovery time objective (RTO) is how long you can afford to be down. Together they decide backup frequency and the disaster-recovery design.
concepts.ref: Recommendations for designing a disaster recovery strategy

concepts.def: Backs up VMs, SQL in VMs, file shares and more into a Recovery Services or Backup vault, with retention policies, soft delete and, with GRS vaults, restores in the paired region.
concepts.ref: What is the Azure Backup service?

concepts.def: Geo-replicate Azure SQL databases to a secondary server in another region, with listener endpoints that keep the same connection string after a failover.
Continuously replicates VMs to another region and orchestrates failover and failback, including recovery plans and test failovers that don't disturb production.
Backup and restore (cheapest, slowest), warm standby (a scaled-down copy in another region), and active-active (both regions serve traffic). Shorter RTO and RPO cost more.
Cosmos DB can accept writes in every region. Concurrent writes to the same item in two regions conflict, and are resolved by last-writer-wins on a timestamp or by your own merge procedure.
concepts.ref: Conflict types and resolution policies when using multiple write regions

concepts.def: Save the business change and the message to publish in the same database transaction (an outbox table or the change feed); a relay then publishes it to the broker. You never save without publishing, or publish without saving.
concepts.ref: Transactional Outbox pattern with Azure Cosmos DB

concepts.def: Scale workers on the work waiting for them, such as queue length or event backlog, instead of CPU. Container Apps uses KEDA scalers for this, including scaling to zero when the queue is empty.
concepts.ref: Set scaling rules in Azure Container Apps

concepts.def: Managed Kubernetes: Azure runs the control plane, and you run node pools of VMs for your pods. Full Kubernetes flexibility, with cluster upgrades, node pools and networking still to operate.
The horizontal pod autoscaler adds pods when load rises; the cluster autoscaler adds nodes when pods can't be scheduled. You need both for a cluster that follows demand.
concepts.ref: Scaling options for applications in AKS

concepts.def: A private registry for container images and artifacts. Clusters and apps pull with their managed identity; Premium adds private endpoints and geo-replication.
Know where every image comes from: import public images into your own registry, scan them, and only let workloads pull from registries you control, with identities rather than passwords.

The Distributed Application Runtime: a sidecar that gives services building blocks such as pub/sub, state and service invocation through a simple HTTP/gRPC API, so code doesn't depend on a specific broker or store SDK.
concepts.ref: Dapr integration with Azure Container Apps

concepts.def: Deploy supporting features (proxies, Dapr, log shippers) as a separate container next to the app container, sharing its lifecycle. The app stays focused; the sidecar can be reused across languages.
Small services, each owning one business capability and its data, deployed independently. Teams move faster and services scale separately, in exchange for distributed-systems complexity.
One public endpoint routes requests to many backend services by path or version, so clients don't need to know where each service lives, and services can move or split without breaking clients.

Each microservice owns its data store, and others reach that data only through its API or events. Services can change schemas and scale independently, at the cost of cross-service queries and consistency.
A business transaction spread over several services as a sequence of local transactions. If a step fails, compensating actions undo the earlier steps (refund the payment, release the stock).
An ordered, persistent log of changes to a container. Functions or other processors read it to update other systems: projections, caches, search indexes or outgoing events.
concepts.ref: Change feed in Azure Cosmos DB

concepts.def: Command and Query Responsibility Segregation: separate the model that handles writes from the model that serves reads, often with the read side as a materialized view in a different store, updated from changes.
Precompute the data a query needs, in the shape it needs, into a separate store kept up to date from changes. Reads become simple and fast; the view lags slightly behind the source.

The Well-Architected pillar about protecting confidentiality, integrity and availability: strong identity, least privilege, encryption, network segmentation and threat detection, designed in from the start.

Microsoft's cloud identity service for employees and apps (formerly Azure Active Directory). It provides sign-in, single sign-on, multifactor authentication, Conditional Access and the tokens apps use to call each other.
Users sign in once with their organisation account and get into every connected app, with central MFA and account lifecycle. When someone leaves, disabling one account removes access everywhere.
App Service can handle sign-in for an app by itself: it redirects to the identity provider, validates tokens and passes the user's identity to your code, with no authentication library to maintain.
concepts.ref: Authentication and authorization in Azure App Service

concepts.def: Customer identity and access management: sign-up and sign-in for consumers and business customers with email, phone or social accounts, with your own branding. The successor to Azure AD B2C for new projects.

Stores secrets, keys and certificates with access control and auditing. Apps read secrets at runtime with their managed identity; soft delete and purge protection prevent accidental or malicious loss of keys.

Services authenticate to each other with Entra ID tokens from managed identities instead of keys, passwords and connection strings. There is nothing to leak or rotate, and access is granted with roles.
Give each identity only the permissions it needs, on only the resources it needs, for only as long as it needs them. A compromised component can then do as little damage as possible.
concepts.ref: Recommendations for identity and access management

concepts.def: APIs must check every bearer token: signature, issuer, audience, expiry and the scopes or roles it grants. Doing it once at the gateway keeps unauthenticated traffic away from the services.
concepts.ref: Protect an API in Azure API Management using OAuth 2.0 authorization with Microsoft Entra ID

concepts.def: Data is encrypted at rest by default with Microsoft-managed keys. With customer-managed keys, the key lives in your Key Vault, so you control rotation and can revoke access to the data by disabling the key.
concepts.ref: Customer-managed keys for Azure Storage encryption

concepts.def: Adaptive mitigation of network-layer floods for public IPs in your virtual networks, with attack telemetry and rapid-response support. Every Azure service gets basic infrastructure protection at no cost.

Never trust a request because of where it comes from. Verify identity explicitly on every request, use least privilege, and assume breach: segment, encrypt and monitor as if attackers are already inside.

Subscriptions are billing and access boundaries for resources; management groups organise subscriptions into a hierarchy. Policies and role assignments set on a management group apply to everything below it.

Rules evaluated against resource configurations: audit what doesn't comply, deny it at creation, or deploy a missing setting automatically. Assigned at a management group, a policy guards every subscription below.
Cloud security posture management (a secure score and recommendations) and workload protection (threat detection for servers, storage, databases, containers and more) across subscriptions.
concepts.ref: What is Microsoft Defender for Cloud?

concepts.def: A cloud SIEM and SOAR built on a Log Analytics workspace: it collects security signals, correlates them into incidents with analytics rules, and automates responses with playbooks.
The central store for Azure Monitor logs. Resources send diagnostic logs and metrics there, you query them with KQL, and alerts, dashboards and Sentinel build on top.

A ready-made environment for application teams: a management group hierarchy, platform subscriptions for connectivity, identity and management, policies as guardrails, and landing-zone subscriptions where apps are deployed.
concepts.ref: What is an Azure landing zone?

concepts.def: The Well-Architected pillar about running the workload well: observability, automation, safe deployments and learning from incidents, so problems are found and fixed before customers notice.
Being able to tell what a system is doing from the outside, through metrics, logs and traces. Good observability means you hear about problems from alerts, not from customers.
concepts.ref: Recommendations for designing and creating a monitoring system

concepts.def: Application performance monitoring in Azure Monitor: requests, dependencies, exceptions, traces and live metrics, collected with OpenTelemetry and stored in a Log Analytics workspace.
Rules that fire when a metric, log query or activity crosses a threshold, and notify an action group: email, SMS, push, webhook, or an automated runbook.
Every request carries a trace id through each service it touches, and each service records timed spans. The result is one end-to-end timeline that shows where a slow request spent its time.
concepts.ref: Distributed tracing and telemetry correlation in Application Insights

concepts.def: A managed search service: full-text, vector and hybrid search with semantic ranking. Indexers pull content from Azure data sources on a schedule and keep the index up to date.
Real-time analytics on event streams with a SQL-like language: filter, join and aggregate events over time windows, and write results to stores, dashboards or alerts.

Streams never end, so aggregates are computed over windows. Tumbling windows are fixed and non-overlapping (per minute); hopping windows overlap; sliding windows move with events; session windows group bursts of activity.
A fast analytics engine for logs, telemetry and time series: ingests large volumes in near real time and answers ad hoc KQL queries over billions of rows in seconds.
Hosted Grafana with Entra ID sign-in and built-in data sources for Azure Monitor and Data Explorer, for operational dashboards without running a Grafana server.
Managed data integration: pipelines that copy and transform data between more than 90 sources and sinks, on schedules or triggers, without servers to manage.
An end-to-end analytics platform: lakehouse, warehouse, data engineering, real-time intelligence and Power BI reports, all working on one copy of the data in OneLake.
Organise a lake in layers: bronze (raw, as ingested), silver (cleaned and conformed) and gold (business-ready aggregates). Each layer is rebuilt from the one before, so raw data is never lost.
concepts.ref: What is the medallion lakehouse architecture?

concepts.def: An Apache Spark-based platform for data engineering, analytics and machine learning on a lakehouse, with notebooks, jobs and Delta Lake tables.
Hosted large language and embedding models in Azure, with Entra ID authentication, private networking and built-in content filtering for prompts and completions.
concepts.ref: What is Azure OpenAI in Azure AI Foundry Models?

concepts.def: Answer questions over your own documents: retrieve the most relevant passages with search, put them in the prompt, and have the model answer from them, citing the sources. The model doesn't need retraining when documents change.
concepts.ref: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) in Azure AI Search

concepts.def: Embeddings turn text into vectors so search can find passages with similar meaning, not just matching words. Hybrid search combines vector and keyword results, and a semantic ranker reorders the best ones.
concepts.ref: Vector search in Azure AI Search

concepts.def: Extracts text, key-value pairs, tables and fields from documents such as invoices, receipts and forms, with prebuilt and custom models. Formerly Form Recognizer.
concepts.ref: What is Azure AI Document Intelligence?

concepts.def: A managed WebSocket service: clients keep a connection open and the server (or other clients, through groups) pushes messages to them in real time, at the scale of hundreds of thousands of connections.
concepts.ref: What is Azure Web PubSub service?

concepts.def: A managed hub for device fleets: per-device identity and authentication, device-to-cloud telemetry at scale, cloud-to-device commands, and message routing to other services.
concepts.ref: IoT concepts and Azure IoT Hub

concepts.def: The Well-Architected pillar about meeting demand efficiently: the right services and sizes, scaling out with load, caching, and testing performance before users do.

When someone posts, write a copy of the post's reference into every follower's precomputed feed, so reading a feed is one cheap lookup. For accounts with millions of followers, skip the fan-out and merge their posts at read time instead (fan-out on read).
Finding things near a point: "drivers within 2 km". Databases index coordinates so these queries stay fast: Redis GEO commands, Cosmos DB spatial indexes, or PostGIS in PostgreSQL.
concepts.ref: Geospatial and GeoJSON location data in Azure Cosmos DB

concepts.def: Containers that run to completion (on demand, on a schedule, or per event) and then stop. They're good for batch work like video transcoding with ffmpeg, now that Azure Media Services is retired.
Split files into chunks identified by a hash of their content. Only changed chunks are uploaded on each sync, identical chunks are stored once, and interrupted uploads resume where they stopped.

Pessimistic locking holds a lock while a booking is in progress, so others wait. Optimistic concurrency lets everyone proceed and rejects a write if the row changed since it was read (an ETag or rowversion check). Optimistic suits low contention; pessimistic suits hot rows.

Deploy many independent copies (stamps) of the whole application stack, each serving a subset of tenants. Stamps cap the blast radius of failures, scale by adding copies, and can be placed in different regions.
Modernize a legacy system piece by piece: put a routing layer in front, send one feature at a time to a new service, and keep the rest on the old system until nothing is left.

A managed SQL Server instance with near-complete compatibility (SQL Agent, cross-database queries, CLR), deployed into your virtual network. The usual target for lifting SQL Server databases with few changes.
concepts.ref: What is Azure SQL Managed Instance?

concepts.def: Deploy the full backend into several regions, each able to serve any user, behind a global entry point and on a globally replicated data store. Users get a nearby region, and losing a region just shifts traffic.
Five pillars for evaluating a design: reliability, security, cost optimization, operational excellence and performance efficiency. Every design is a set of trade-offs between them.

challenges.title: Hello, Azure
challenges.brief:
A designer wants a personal portfolio site: a dozen pages of project write-ups and images, and a link to email them. Most visitors arrive from a link in a CV, some from other countries.

They never want to patch a server, and while traffic is low the site should cost next to nothing.
functional: Visitors open the portfolio in a web browser
Pages and images load from Azure
nonFunctional: Every page is served over HTTPS
No servers or operating systems to patch
Costs as little as possible while traffic is low
Loads quickly for visitors in other countries

estimate.q: About how much data does the site send to visitors per month?
estimate.workings: 2,000 visits × 4 pages × 1.5 MB = 12,000 MB ≈ 12 GB per month.

tradeoff.q: Why is Static Web Apps a better fit than a virtual machine for this site?
choices: Azure runs and patches the servers and serves the files from locations around the world, so there is nothing to look after.
Virtual machines can't serve HTTPS.
Static Web Apps can run any server-side software a virtual machine can.
tradeoff.why: A VM means an operating system to patch, a web server to configure and a bill even when nobody visits. For a handful of static pages, a managed host removes all of that.

challenges.learn:
For static content, the simplest and cheapest host is one where Azure runs the servers: **Static Web Apps** serves the files from points of presence worldwide, with HTTPS included.

**App Service** fits when the site needs server-side code, but you then choose a plan tier and make sure HTTPS-only is on. The trade-off is control: a managed platform decides the operating system, runtime and scaling options for you.

rules.text: The site runs on a managed web platform, with no servers to patch
rules.hint: Look for a service where Azure runs the servers and you only bring the files or the code.

rules.text: Visitors' browsers load the pages from that platform
rules.hint: Connect the browser to the service that hosts the site, in the direction of the request.

rules.text: Every page is served over HTTPS
rules.hint: Static Web Apps always uses HTTPS. App Service has an HTTPS-only setting: make sure it is on.

rules.text: Pages are served from locations close to visitors around the world
rules.hint: Some hosts copy static files to many locations worldwide on their own.

rules.text: The whole design costs at most 1 unit while traffic is low
rules.hint: Free and entry tiers exist for exactly this kind of site.

rules.text: No virtual machine to patch and restart
rules.hint: A virtual machine brings an operating system you must update, secure and monitor yourself.

challenges.title: Remember my tasks
challenges.brief:
A small team built a to-do app prototype that keeps tasks in the browser, so they vanish when people switch laptops. They want tasks saved on the server, per user, and visible on every device.

They are happy writing a small web API and want a managed relational database.
functional: Create, complete and delete tasks
See the same tasks from any device
nonFunctional: Tasks are never lost when a browser is closed
The database is not reachable straight from browsers
No database passwords in the app settings

estimate.q: Roughly how much task data is stored?

tradeoff.q: Why put a web API between the browser and the database?
choices: The API checks who the user is and what they may change, and the database stays private.
Browsers can't speak HTTPS to databases.
It makes every query faster.
tradeoff.why: A database exposed to browsers would need credentials in client code that anyone can read. The API is where authorization, validation and business rules live.

challenges.learn:
The classic **three-tier** shape: the browser talks to an API on **App Service**, and only the API talks to **Azure SQL Database**. The extra hop costs a few milliseconds but gives you one place to check permissions and keeps the database off the internet.

Use a **managed identity** for the API → database connection so there is no password to leak or rotate.

rules.text: An API runs on a managed compute service
rules.hint: Something has to receive the browser's requests and run your code, without a server to patch.

rules.text: Tasks are stored in a managed database
rules.hint: Browsers forget; a database keeps data safe, backed up and shared across devices.

rules.text: Browsers reach the data only through the API
rules.hint: Draw the request from the browser to your code, then from your code to the database.

rules.text: The API signs in to the database with a managed identity
rules.hint: Look at the authentication setting on the connection into the database.

rules.text: The API accepts HTTPS only
rules.hint: App Service has an HTTPS-only setting.

rules.text: Browsers don't connect straight to the database
rules.hint: A database open to browsers puts its credentials in code anyone can read.

challenges.title: Your own name
challenges.brief:
A local bakery runs its ordering site on App Service at a default azurewebsites.net address. They bought their own domain and want customers to type that name and always land on a secure page with a padlock.

Nobody on the team wants to buy or renew certificates by hand.
functional: Customers open the site using the bakery's own domain
The site keeps taking orders as before
nonFunctional: Every request uses HTTPS; plain HTTP is redirected
Certificates renew automatically
The domain's DNS records are managed in Azure

tradeoff.q: What does a managed certificate save the bakery from?
choices: Buying, installing and renewing a certificate before it expires.
Configuring DNS records for the domain.
Paying for the App Service plan.
tradeoff.why: Expired certificates are a classic outage. A managed certificate is issued and renewed by the platform; DNS still has to point the name at the app.

challenges.learn:
A public **Azure DNS** zone holds the domain's records (a CNAME or A record pointing at the app, plus a TXT record that proves ownership). App Service then binds the custom domain and issues a free **managed certificate** that it renews on its own.

Turn on **HTTPS only** so plain HTTP is redirected. The trade-off: managed certificates cover common cases (no wildcard names), and you still own the DNS records.

rules.text: The domain's records live in a public DNS zone in Azure
rules.hint: People on the internet need to resolve the name. Which kind of zone answers them?

rules.text: Browsers reach the ordering site
rules.hint: Keep the request path from the browser to the app.

rules.text: The site accepts HTTPS only
rules.hint: App Service redirects plain HTTP when one setting is on.

rules.text: The certificate is issued and renewed by the platform
rules.hint: App Service can create a free certificate for your custom domain.

rules.text: The diagram shows browsers resolving the name in Azure DNS
rules.hint: Before the browser connects, it looks the name up.

rules.text: The whole design costs at most 3 units
rules.hint: A custom domain and certificate don't need a bigger plan.

challenges.title: Pictures go in Blob
challenges.brief:
A recipe site lets cooks publish recipes with up to ten step-by-step photos each. The first version stored photos inside the database, and backups now take hours and the database bill keeps climbing.

They want recipes in a database, photos somewhere built for files, and photos that load quickly for readers abroad.
functional: Publish a recipe with photos
Readers browse recipes and see the photos
nonFunctional: Photos are not stored in the relational database
Photos load quickly for readers in other countries
The app reads and writes storage without account keys

estimate.q: About how much photo storage is needed?

tradeoff.q: Why move photos out of the database into Blob Storage?
choices: Blob Storage is far cheaper per gigabyte and serves files over HTTP; the database stays small and fast to back up.
Databases can't store binary data.
Blob Storage supports SQL joins on images.
tradeoff.why: Databases can hold blobs, but every byte then goes through expensive database storage, backups and the app. Object storage is built for large files.

challenges.learn:
Store files in **Blob Storage** and keep only their names or URLs in the database. The database shrinks, backups speed up, and photos can be served straight from storage, or better, cached by **Front Door** close to readers.

The trade-off: the recipe and its photos now live in two stores, so deleting a recipe must clean up both.

rules.text: Recipes are served by an app on a managed platform
rules.hint: Readers and cooks talk to your code first.

rules.text: Recipe text lives in a database
rules.hint: Titles, ingredients and steps are small structured rows.

rules.text: Photos are stored in Blob Storage
rules.hint: Object storage is the cheap, durable place for files.

rules.text: Readers' browsers can load the photos from storage
rules.hint: Draw how a photo travels from storage to the reader, directly or through an edge service.

rules.text: Photos are cached at the edge close to readers
rules.hint: A global edge service can cache static files near readers.

rules.text: The app writes to storage with a managed identity
rules.hint: Check the authentication on the connection from the app to Blob Storage.

challenges.title: Valet key
challenges.brief:
A community app lets members upload a profile photo of up to 10 MB. Today every upload streams through the API, which ties up its instances and doubles the bandwidth.

The team wants phones to upload straight to storage, with the API only deciding who may upload where, and saving the photo's address.
functional: A member uploads a profile photo
The member's profile shows the new photo
nonFunctional: Photo bytes never pass through the API
Upload permission is short-lived and limited to one file
No storage account key ever leaves Azure

estimate.q: How much upload traffic stops passing through the API each day?
estimate.workings: 40,000 uploads × 4 MB = 160,000 MB ≈ 160 GB per day.

tradeoff.q: What does the API hand the phone in the Valet Key pattern?
choices: A short-lived SAS that allows writing one blob, and nothing else.
The storage account key, so the phone can upload any file.
A copy of the photo, to upload on the phone's behalf.
tradeoff.why: The valet key opens one door for a short time. Account keys open everything forever, and proxying the bytes is what the pattern avoids.

challenges.learn:
With the **Valet Key** pattern the API checks the user, then returns a **SAS** limited to one blob, write-only, for a few minutes. The phone uploads straight to Blob Storage, and the API only stores the photo's name in the database.

Sign the SAS with a **user delegation key** (obtained with the API's managed identity) rather than the account key. The trade-off: you must validate uploads afterwards (size, type, malware), because the API never sees the bytes.

rules.text: Phones upload photos straight to Blob Storage with a SAS
rules.hint: The connection from the client to storage carries a short-lived token.

rules.text: An API decides who may upload and hands out the token
rules.hint: The client still asks your code for permission first.

rules.text: The photo's address is saved with the profile
rules.hint: Profiles live in a database; the photo itself does not.

rules.text: The API talks to storage with its managed identity (user delegation SAS)
rules.hint: A SAS can be signed with a key obtained through Entra ID instead of the account key.

rules.text: The API reaches the database with a managed identity
rules.hint: No passwords on any connection your code makes.

rules.text: Clients never hold a storage account key
rules.hint: An account key in a phone app gives anyone full control of the storage account.

challenges.title: Two instances, one login
challenges.brief:
A booking site on App Service added a second instance for the busy season. Since then, some customers are logged out mid-booking and lose their basket, especially during deployments.

Sessions are kept in the memory of whichever instance served the login.
functional: Customers log in and keep a basket while booking
The site runs on more than one instance
nonFunctional: Losing or restarting one instance logs nobody out
Any instance can serve any request
Capacity can grow with demand

estimate.q: How much memory do all sessions need in a shared store?

tradeoff.q: Why not just keep session affinity ("sticky sessions") on?
choices: Users stuck to an instance are still logged out when it restarts, and load spreads unevenly.
Session affinity is not available on App Service.
Affinity makes the site use HTTP instead of HTTPS.
tradeoff.why: Affinity hides the problem until an instance is recycled or scaled in. An external session store fixes the cause.

challenges.learn:
Keep the web tier **stateless**: store sessions in **Azure Managed Redis**, turn **session affinity (ARR)** off, and run at least two instances. Any instance can then serve any request, and scaling or patching doesn't log anyone out.

The trade-off is a network hop to Redis on each request (well under a millisecond) and one more service to run.

rules.text: The site runs on at least two instances
rules.hint: Instance count is a setting on the App Service plan.

rules.text: Sessions live in a shared in-memory store
rules.hint: Instances need a common place to read sessions from.

rules.text: Session affinity is off so load spreads evenly
rules.hint: App Service pins users to one instance unless you turn ARR affinity off.

rules.text: Bookings are saved in a database
rules.hint: Baskets are temporary; bookings are not.

rules.text: Instance count grows with demand automatically
rules.hint: Autoscale needs a Standard plan or higher.

rules.text: The app reaches Redis and the database with a managed identity
rules.hint: Azure Managed Redis and Azure SQL both accept Entra ID tokens.

challenges.title: Night shift
challenges.brief:
A shop owner wants yesterday's sales summary in their inbox at 6:00 every morning: totals, top products and refunds, read from the existing orders database.

The job runs for about two minutes a day. They don't want a server running the other 23 hours and 58 minutes.
functional: Every morning, read yesterday's orders
Email a summary to the owner
nonFunctional: Runs on a schedule with no one pressing a button
Costs almost nothing between runs
No database password stored in the job's settings

estimate.q: How many minutes per month does the job actually run?
estimate.workings: 30 runs × 2 minutes = 60 minutes, out of about 43,200 in a month.

tradeoff.q: Why a timer-triggered function rather than a small always-on VM with a cron job?
choices: You pay for about an hour of execution a month instead of a server all month, and there's no OS to patch.
VMs can't send email.
Functions run faster than VMs.
tradeoff.why: For short scheduled work, serverless costs track the work, not the clock. A VM would sit idle 99.9% of the time.

challenges.learn:
A **timer trigger** (a CRON expression) runs an **Azure Function** each morning. It reads the orders with a **managed identity** and sends the email through **Communication Services**. On the Flex Consumption plan nothing runs between executions.

The trade-off: a cold start adds a few seconds, which nobody notices at 6:00, and very long jobs belong in a container job instead.

rules.text: A scheduled function runs the report
rules.hint: Functions start on a trigger. Which trigger fires at a fixed time?

rules.text: The job reads the orders database
rules.hint: Connect the scheduled job to where orders live.

rules.text: The summary is sent by an email service
rules.hint: Azure has an API for email and SMS.

rules.text: The job reads the database with a managed identity
rules.hint: Look at the authentication on the connection into the database.

rules.text: The function app uses the Flex Consumption plan
rules.hint: The current serverless plan for new function apps bills per execution.

rules.text: No server waits all day for a two-minute job
rules.hint: A VM bills every hour whether or not the job is running.

challenges.title: Money's in
challenges.brief:
An online course shop takes card payments through a payment provider. When a payment succeeds, the provider calls a webhook so the shop can unlock the course.

The provider retries any call that doesn't get a quick success response, and last month some customers were charged once but got two enrolment emails and two invoices.
functional: Receive payment-succeeded webhooks
Unlock the course exactly once per payment
nonFunctional: A repeated webhook has no extra effect
The endpoint answers quickly so the provider stops retrying
The webhook signing secret is not in the code

tradeoff.q: How should the handler deal with the same payment event arriving twice?
choices: Record each event id and skip ids it has already processed.
Ask the provider to never retry.
Process it twice and refund the extra invoice later.
tradeoff.why: At-least-once delivery is the norm for webhooks. Idempotency on the receiving side is the only reliable fix.

challenges.learn:
Expose the webhook as an **HTTP-triggered function** that verifies the provider's signature, then makes the work **idempotent**: store the event id with the enrolment in one transaction, and treat a repeat id as already done.

Keep the signing secret in **Key Vault**. The trade-off: idempotency needs a durable record of processed ids, a little extra storage and a lookup per call.

rules.text: The payment provider calls an HTTP-triggered function
rules.hint: Webhooks arrive as HTTPS requests. Which trigger handles those?

rules.text: The handler is idempotent
rules.hint: Retries will deliver the same event again. Mark the handler as safe to repeat.

rules.text: Enrolments and processed event ids are saved in a database
rules.hint: Idempotency needs a durable record of what was already handled.

rules.text: The signing secret is read from Key Vault
rules.hint: Secrets belong in a vault, read at runtime.

rules.text: The function reaches its data with a managed identity
rules.hint: Check the authentication on the function's outgoing connections.

challenges.title: Pick the compute
challenges.brief:
A ticket-scanning API for small venues is already packaged as a container. It gets bursts of thousands of requests in the hour before events and almost nothing overnight.

The two-person team has no Kubernetes experience and wants to pay as little as possible while it sits idle.
functional: Scanners call the API to validate tickets
The API reads tickets from a database
nonFunctional: Scales out quickly for pre-event bursts
Costs next to nothing when idle
No cluster or servers for the team to operate

estimate.q: How many replicas are needed at peak?

tradeoff.q: Which compute fits best: VMs, App Service, Container Apps or AKS?
choices: Container Apps: it runs the existing container, scales on HTTP traffic and can scale to zero, with no cluster to manage.
AKS: Kubernetes is the only way to run containers.
Virtual machines: they are the cheapest when idle.
App Service: it scales to zero replicas overnight.
tradeoff.why: AKS brings a cluster to operate, VMs bill around the clock, and App Service plans keep at least one instance running. Container Apps matches bursty, containerized, small-team work.

challenges.learn:
**Container Apps** runs the existing image with an **HTTP scale rule**: replicas are added as concurrent requests grow and removed down to **zero** when idle, so overnight costs almost nothing.

The trade-off of scaling to zero is a **cold start** on the first request; set `minReplicas` to 1 when that matters more than the idle cost.

rules.text: Scanners call a serverless container platform
rules.hint: The API is already a container, and nobody wants to run a cluster.

rules.text: The API scales to zero when idle
rules.hint: The minimum replica count decides what you pay overnight.

rules.text: Replicas scale on HTTP traffic
rules.hint: Pick the scale rule that reacts to incoming requests.

rules.text: The API can reach the replicas needed at peak
rules.hint: Check your estimate against the maximum replica count.

rules.text: Tickets are read from a database
rules.hint: The API needs somewhere to look tickets up.

rules.text: The API reads the database with a managed identity
rules.hint: No connection strings in the container's environment.

rules.text: No virtual machines to run
rules.hint: VMs bill all night and need patching.

challenges.title: Pastebin
challenges.brief:
Build a service for sharing text snippets: paste some text, get a short link, share it. Snippets can be up to 1 MB, most are read a few times, and a few go viral on forums.

The site must stay up when one server fails and load quickly worldwide.
functional: Create a paste and get a short link
Open a paste by its link
Pastes can expire after a chosen time
nonFunctional: Survives the loss of one app instance
Popular pastes load quickly anywhere in the world
Large paste bodies don't bloat the database
No secrets in app settings

estimate.q: How much new paste data arrives per year?
estimate.workings: 1M pastes/day × 10 KB = 10 GB/day; × 365 days ≈ 3,650 GB ≈ 3.65 TB.

estimate.q: Average paste reads per second?

tradeoff.q: Why split each paste between a database row and a blob?
choices: Small metadata (id, owner, expiry) is queried; large bodies are just stored and fetched, which object storage does cheaply.
Databases can't hold text larger than 1 KB.
Blob Storage can't store small files.
tradeoff.why: Metadata needs indexes and queries; bodies need cheap capacity. Splitting them keeps each store doing what it's good at.

challenges.learn:
Pastebin is the "metadata + blobs" pattern: a small row per paste in **Azure SQL** or **Cosmos DB**, the body in **Blob Storage**, and stateless app instances (at least two) behind **Front Door**, which also caches viral pastes at the edge.

The trade-off: caching makes deletes and expiry eventually visible, so set short cache lifetimes or purge on delete.

rules.text: Readers come in through a global edge service
rules.hint: Readers are worldwide; put a global HTTP entry point in front of the app.

rules.text: The app runs on at least two instances
rules.hint: One instance is a single point of failure.

rules.text: Paste metadata is kept in a database
rules.hint: Ids, owners and expiry dates are small and queried often.

rules.text: Paste bodies are kept in Blob Storage
rules.hint: Large text bodies are cheaper in object storage.

rules.text: Viral pastes are cached at the edge
rules.hint: The edge service can cache responses.

rules.text: Every connection from the app to data uses a managed identity
rules.hint: Check each connection from your app into a data store.

rules.text: Paste bodies survive the loss of an availability zone
rules.hint: Storage redundancy has zone-redundant options.

challenges.title: Read-heavy blog
challenges.brief: A blogging platform runs on PostgreSQL. Readers outnumber writers a hundred to one, and at peak the single database server is pegged at 100% CPU serving page reads, which also slows down authors saving drafts.
functional: Authors write and publish posts
Readers read posts and comments
nonFunctional: Reads scale beyond one server
Writes stay on one authoritative copy
A replica that lags a second or two behind is acceptable for readers

estimate.q: How many database servers (primary included) are needed for peak reads?
estimate.workings: 2,400 reads/s ÷ 1,000 per server = 2.4, so 3 servers: the primary plus 2 read replicas.

tradeoff.q: What do readers give up when their reads go to a replica?
choices: A new comment may take a moment to appear, because replication is asynchronous.
Replicas can't run SELECT queries.
Readers can no longer use HTTPS.
tradeoff.why: Replica lag is the price of scaling reads. Authors should read their own drafts from the primary.

challenges.learn:
Add **read replicas** to Azure Database for PostgreSQL and route reads to them; writes keep going to the primary, which replicates asynchronously. That scales reads almost linearly.

The trade-off is **replication lag**: replicas can be slightly behind, so screens that must show the latest write (an author's editor) still read from the primary.

rules.text: Posts live in a managed PostgreSQL server
rules.hint: The team already runs PostgreSQL.

rules.text: There are at least two read replicas
rules.hint: Your estimate says how many servers the reads need.

rules.text: The primary replicates to each replica
rules.hint: Use replication connections from the primary to the replicas.

rules.text: The app sends reads to the replicas
rules.hint: Connect the app to the replicas for its read queries.

rules.text: The app still writes to the primary
rules.hint: Replicas are read-only.

rules.text: The primary survives the loss of an availability zone
rules.hint: Flexible server has a zone-redundant high availability option.

rules.text: The app signs in to the databases with a managed identity
rules.hint: PostgreSQL flexible server accepts Entra ID authentication.

challenges.title: Cart in a flash
challenges.brief:
A fashion retailer's shopping cart is read on every page view and changed a few times per visit. Each cart belongs to one signed-in user, and every lookup is "get this user's cart".

The team wants single-digit-millisecond reads at any scale, without managing database servers.
functional: Add and remove items in a cart
Show the cart on every page
nonFunctional: Cart reads under 10 ms
Throughput scales with traffic
Every lookup goes to a single partition

numbers.label: Cart reads per second at peak (assume)
Assume a 1 KB point read costs

estimate.q: How many RU/s do cart reads need at peak?

tradeoff.q: Why is /userId a good partition key for carts?
choices: Every lookup includes it, there are millions of distinct values, and load spreads evenly.
It keeps all carts in a single partition, which is fastest.
Partition keys must always be called userId.
tradeoff.why: A key that appears in every query and has high cardinality gives single-partition point reads and no hot spots.

challenges.learn:
Store carts in **Cosmos DB for NoSQL** with **/userId** as the partition key. Every read is then a point read (id + partition key, about 1 RU), and millions of users spread evenly across partitions.

The trade-off: queries that don't include the partition key fan out to every partition and cost far more, so pick the key from your access pattern, not from the data model.

rules.text: Carts live in Cosmos DB for NoSQL
rules.hint: You want a managed NoSQL store with single-digit-millisecond reads.

rules.text: Carts are partitioned by user
rules.hint: Every lookup is "this user's cart". Set the partition key to the field each lookup uses (for example /userId).

rules.text: The shop's API reads and writes carts
rules.hint: Connect the app to the database.

rules.text: Throughput follows traffic automatically
rules.hint: Cosmos DB can scale RU/s between a floor and a ceiling.

rules.text: The API uses a managed identity for Cosmos DB
rules.hint: Cosmos DB supports Entra ID role-based access for data.

challenges.title: Hot partition
challenges.brief:
A multi-tenant audit-log service stores events in Cosmos DB partitioned by /tenantId. One enterprise tenant now produces most of the events. Its writes are throttled while the other partitions sit idle, and its partition is heading for the storage limit of a single logical partition.

Fix the data design. Queries are almost always "events for tenant X", often narrowed to one user.
functional: Ingest audit events for every tenant
Query a tenant's events, optionally by user
nonFunctional: No single partition key takes most of the writes
Tenant-scoped queries stay efficient
Throughput follows load

numbers.label: Assume one logical partition holds at most

estimate.q: How many RU/s do all writes need?
How many days until the big tenant's single partition key value reaches 20 GB?
estimate.workings: 100 writes/s × 1 KB = 100 KB/s × 86,400 s ≈ 8.64 GB/day; 20 GB ÷ 8.64 GB/day ≈ 2.3 days.

tradeoff.q: Why does a hierarchical key (tenantId, then userId) beat a plain /userId key here?
choices: A big tenant spreads over many partitions, while queries for one tenant still go only to that tenant's partitions.
It uses fewer RUs for every write.
Plain /userId keys aren't allowed in Cosmos DB.
tradeoff.why: /userId alone spreads load but turns every "events for tenant X" query into a fan-out across all partitions. Hierarchical keys keep tenant-level routing.

challenges.learn:
A partition key with one dominant value creates a **hot partition**: throughput is spread across physical partitions, so one busy key gets throttled while the rest idle, and a logical partition can't grow past its size limit.

**Hierarchical partition keys** (tenantId → userId) let a large tenant span many partitions while tenant queries stay targeted. A synthetic key such as tenantId-userId also spreads load, but tenant-wide queries then fan out.

rules.text: No single tenant's writes land on one partition key value
rules.hint: Add a second level under the tenant, or use a key with many more distinct values.

rules.text: Events are still stored in Cosmos DB
rules.hint: Keep the database, fix its design.

rules.text: Tenants send events through the API
rules.hint: Keep the API in front of the database.

rules.text: The key is hierarchical, so tenant queries stay targeted
rules.hint: Cosmos DB supports up to three levels in a partition key.

rules.text: Throughput scales with load
rules.hint: Spiky ingestion is a good fit for autoscale throughput.

challenges.title: Pick a consistency
challenges.brief:
A news site's editors publish and correct articles in a CMS backed by Cosmos DB, replicated to three regions for readers worldwide. Editors complain that right after saving a correction, they sometimes still see the old text.

Readers don't mind seeing a correction a second late. Editors must always see their own edits.
functional: Editors save and immediately re-read articles
Readers worldwide read articles
nonFunctional: An editor always reads their own latest write
Reads stay fast in every region
Don't pay for stronger guarantees than needed

numbers.label: Assume reads at strong or bounded staleness cost

tradeoff.q: Which consistency level gives editors read-your-own-writes at the lowest cost?
choices: Session
Strong
Eventual
Consistent prefix
tradeoff.why: Session guarantees read-your-writes within a client session, with single-region-like read cost. Strong and bounded staleness also do it but cost twice the RUs and add latency; eventual and consistent prefix don't guarantee it.

challenges.learn:
Cosmos DB's five **consistency levels** trade freshness for latency, availability and cost. **Session** consistency guarantees each client reads its own writes, which is exactly what editors need, while readers elsewhere get fast local reads.

**Strong** would also work but makes every read cost twice the RUs, and writes wait for the other regions. Choose the weakest level that meets the requirement.

rules.text: Articles are stored in Cosmos DB
rules.hint: The CMS already uses Cosmos DB.

rules.text: Editors always read their own writes
rules.hint: Only some consistency levels guarantee read-your-writes.

rules.text: Articles are replicated to the readers' regions
rules.hint: Readers are on three continents.

rules.text: The CMS and the site read through an app tier
rules.hint: Connect clients to an app, and the app to the database.

rules.text: The cheapest level that meets the requirement is used
rules.hint: Strong and bounded staleness reads cost twice as much.

rules.text: The app uses a managed identity for Cosmos DB
rules.hint: No account keys in app settings.

rules.text: No strong consistency across three regions
rules.hint: Strong consistency makes writes wait for other regions and doubles read cost.

challenges.title: Many small tenants
challenges.brief: A scheduling SaaS gives each of its 300 customer businesses its own Azure SQL database for isolation. Each database is idle most of the day and spikes briefly when that business opens. Sizing every database for its own peak is getting expensive.
functional: Each tenant keeps its own database

challenges.brief:
A social app caches each profile for exactly 10 minutes. When a celebrity's profile expires, tens of thousands of requests miss at the same instant, all query the database, and the database falls over. A few minutes later the same thing happens on the hour, when thousands of keys loaded together expire together.

Fix the caching without removing the cache.

nonFunctional: An expiring hot key sends one query to the database, not thousands

tradeoff.q: Why add random jitter to TTLs?

It stops keys from ever expiring.
tradeoff.why: Identical TTLs line up expirations. A few percent of randomness turns one spike into a gentle slope.

A **cache stampede** happens when a hot key expires and every request reloads it at once. Protect against it by letting a single request refresh the key (a short lock or early refresh) while the others wait or get the old value, and by adding **TTL jitter** so keys loaded together don't expire together.

The trade-off: some users briefly see a slightly stale profile, which is far better than a database outage.

tradeoff.q: Why does LFU beat LRU for this workload?
choices: LFU keeps items read often over time; LRU keeps whatever was touched last, so one crawler pass can evict the best-sellers.

When the cache is full, the **eviction policy** decides what goes. **LRU** removes the least recently used keys, which suits recency-driven access. **LFU** removes the least frequently used, so a crawler touching each product once can't push out items that are hot all day.

Never use **noeviction** for a disposable cache: when memory fills, writes start failing. The trade-off of LFU: a newly popular item needs a few hits before it's protected.

challenges.title: Breaking news
challenges.brief:
A news site normally serves about 2,000 requests a second. When big news breaks, traffic jumps 50× within five minutes and stays there for an hour or two. Last time the site went down during the most-read hour of the year.

The owners won't pay for 50× capacity all year round.

nonFunctional: Survives a 50× spike within five minutes

estimate.workings: 100,000 × (1 − 0.98) = 2,000 requests/s, the same as a normal day.

tradeoff.q: Why not simply run enough instances for the peak all year?
choices: You would pay for 50× capacity that sits idle almost all the time; edge caching and autoscale handle the spike for a fraction of the cost.
Azure doesn't allow that many instances.
More instances make each request slower.
tradeoff.why: Caching cuts the load that reaches the origin; autoscale covers the rest only while the spike lasts.

challenges.learn:
Absorb spikes in layers: **Front Door caching** answers most article reads at the edge, **Redis** shields the database from the remaining misses (with **stampede protection** so a hot story doesn't melt it), and **autoscale** adds app instances only while the spike lasts.

The trade-off is freshness: cached pages lag behind updates by their TTL, so use short TTLs for the home page and purge an article when it's corrected.

A real-estate portal runs two VM pools in one region: an API pool and an image-resizing pool that needs much bigger machines. Both are served from one hostname: /api/* must go to the API pool and /images/* to the image pool.

VNet integration encrypts SQL traffic.
Private endpoints only accept traffic from VMs.
tradeoff.why: Private endpoints are inbound doors in your VNet. The caller has to be in (or integrated with) that network to use them.

The trade-offs: more networking to manage (subnets, DNS), and every tool that used the public endpoint (developers' laptops, CI pipelines) now needs a private path too.

It moves the VMs to a different region.
tradeoff.why: Removing the public IP removes the attack surface. Bastion is the managed jump point inside the VNet.

challenges.brief: A retailer runs three line-of-business apps, each in its own virtual network managed by a different team. Security wants every app's outbound internet traffic inspected and logged in one place, by one central team, without buying three firewalls.

choices: A little latency and a shared dependency: if the hub is misconfigured, every spoke is affected.

tradeoff.why: Centralizing inspection creates a critical shared component. Make it zone-redundant and change it carefully.

In **hub and spoke**, a hub VNet holds shared services such as **Azure Firewall** (in its own subnet), and each app gets a spoke VNet peered to the hub. A route table on each spoke subnet sends 0.0.0.0/0 to the firewall, so all egress is inspected and logged once.

The trade-off: the hub is a critical shared dependency, and traffic takes an extra hop. Virtual WAN is the managed alternative when hubs multiply.

A bank is launching a public loan-application site. Move slow, failure-prone side work off the request path: the API writes the user, drops a message on a **Service Bus queue** and returns. A **queue-triggered function** sends the email through **Communication Services**, and Service Bus redelivers the message if sending fails.

The trade-off is eventual completion: the email is "on its way", not "sent", when the user sees the welcome screen.

tradeoff.q: Why a topic rather than three queues the order service writes to?
choices: With a topic the publisher sends once; adding a subscriber is configuration, not a change to the order service.
Topics deliver messages faster than queues.

tradeoff.why: Three queues still couple the publisher to the list of consumers. A topic moves that list into subscriptions.

challenges.learn:
With **Publisher-Subscriber**, the order service publishes one "order placed" message to a **Service Bus topic**. Each consumer (email, SMS, analytics) has its own **subscription** and processes its copy at its own pace. A loyalty service later is just a new subscription.

The trade-off: nobody sees the whole flow in one place, so invest in tracing, and remember that topics need the Standard tier or higher.

An invoicing worker reads invoice requests from a Service Bus queue. One malformed message crashes the worker every time; it's redelivered again and again, burning compute and delaying every invoice behind it. Someone once raised the queue's max delivery count to the maximum "so nothing gets lost".

Fix it so bad messages are set aside after a few tries and someone can inspect them, while good invoices keep flowing.

choices: A deleted invoice is lost; the dead-letter queue keeps it for inspection and replay once the bug is fixed.
Service Bus can't delete messages.

challenges.learn:
Set a sensible **max delivery count** (the default is 10): after that many failed attempts, Service Bus moves the message to the queue's **dead-letter subqueue**, so the worker moves on. Add a consumer that reads the **dead-letter** subqueue, stores the messages for inspection, and alerts someone.

The trade-off: transient failures need retries too, so don't set the count so low that a brief outage dead-letters good messages.

challenges.title: Order matters
challenges.brief:
A bank's ledger service receives account events (deposit, withdrawal, fee, close) through a queue. Several workers process messages in parallel, and sometimes a withdrawal is processed before the deposit that funds it, so a valid transaction is rejected.

Events for the same account must be processed in order, while different accounts are still processed in parallel.

Throughput keeps up with peaks

tradeoff.q: Why not use a single worker to guarantee order?
choices: One worker gives global order but no parallelism; sessions keep order per account and still let many workers run.
A single worker can't read Service Bus.
Order is guaranteed by default in every queue.
tradeoff.why: Global ordering is rarely needed. Ordering per key (per account) scales because keys are independent.

challenges.learn:
Service Bus **sessions** implement the **Sequential Convoy** pattern: the sender sets the session id to the account number, and each session is locked to one consumer, which receives that account's messages in order. Different sessions are spread across many competing consumers.

The trade-off: one slow or stuck account only delays itself, but a very busy account can't be processed faster than one consumer allows. Sessions need the Standard tier or higher.

challenges.title: No double invoices
challenges.brief:
A subscription business sends "create invoice" messages from its billing app to a Service Bus queue. Two things go wrong: the billing app resends a message when an acknowledgement times out, and the worker sometimes crashes after writing an invoice but before completing the message, so it gets the message again.

Customers are receiving duplicate invoices.

choices: Duplicate detection drops resends from the sender, but a message redelivered to a worker after a crash is the same message; only the worker can recognise it.

It isn't needed; duplicate detection covers every case.
tradeoff.why: Two different sources of duplicates need two defences: one at the broker, one in the consumer.

challenges.learn:
Use both defences. **Duplicate detection** on the queue drops a message whose MessageId (set to the invoice request id) was already received in the detection window, which catches sender resends. An **idempotent consumer** records processed request ids in the same transaction as the invoice, which catches redeliveries after crashes.

The trade-off: the detection window costs broker throughput, and the idempotency table needs its own clean-up.

Every remote call needs a **timeout** (seconds, not the 100-second default), a few **retries** for transient errors, **exponential backoff** between them, and **jitter** so thousands of clients don't retry in lockstep.

The trade-off: retries multiply load on a failing dependency (here up to 4×), and they're only safe for idempotent operations, so buy labels with an idempotency key. When failures persist, a circuit breaker should stop the retries altogether.

choices: Redundancy copies every change, including deletions and ransomware encryption; a backup keeps older versions you can go back to.
Geo-redundant storage is slower.
Backups and redundancy are the same thing.
tradeoff.why: Redundancy protects against hardware and site failures. Backups protect against bad changes.

challenges.learn:
Match tools to targets. Azure SQL **point-in-time restore** meets the one-hour **RPO**, and **long-term retention (LTR)** keeps monthly backups for seven years. An **Azure Backup** vault with **GRS** backs up the VMs daily and allows cross-region restore. Blob **versioning** recovers overwritten or deleted documents.

The trade-off: retention costs storage, and a backup you've never restored is a hope, not a plan. Test restores regularly.

challenges.title: Standby region
challenges.brief:
An insurer's claims portal runs in one region. The regulator now requires that it can be running in another region within 30 minutes of a regional disaster, losing at most a few seconds of claims data.

The business won't pay for two full-size live regions; a smaller warm standby is fine.
functional: Claimants use one URL in either region
The standby region can take over
nonFunctional: RTO of 30 minutes
RPO of seconds for the claims database
The secondary region runs a scaled-down copy
Traffic moves to the standby only when the primary fails

tradeoff.q: Warm standby vs active-active: what do you save and what do you give up?
choices: You pay for a smaller second region and keep data in one writable place, but failover takes minutes and the standby must scale up.
Warm standby has no data loss and instant failover.
Active-active is always cheaper.
tradeoff.why: Warm standby balances cost and recovery time. Active-active cuts RTO to near zero at roughly double the cost and harder data consistency.

challenges.learn:
A **warm standby**: **Front Door** with **priority routing** sends everyone to the primary and switches to the secondary when health probes fail. An Azure SQL **failover group** geo-replicates the database, and its listener keeps the same connection string after failover. The secondary app runs at reduced size and scales up on failover.

The trade-offs: replication is asynchronous (seconds of RPO), failover takes minutes, and the plan only works if you rehearse it. For VM-based apps, **Site Recovery** replicates the VMs instead.
