challenges.title: Both regions live
challenges.brief:
A warehouse network tracks stock counts for shelves in Europe and North America. Pickers on both continents update counts constantly and need fast local writes, and the system must keep accepting updates if either region goes down.

With last-writer-wins, two pickers decrementing the same shelf at once lost one of the updates, and the stock went wrong.
functional: Pickers update stock counts from either continent
Both regions serve reads and writes
nonFunctional: Writes are local in both regions
Either region can fail without stopping updates
Concurrent updates to the same shelf are merged, not lost

tradeoff.q: Why is last-writer-wins the wrong policy for stock counts?
choices: Two concurrent decrements conflict; LWW keeps one and silently drops the other, so the count is wrong. A custom merge can apply both.
LWW is not available with multi-region writes.
LWW makes writes slower.
tradeoff.why: LWW is fine when the latest value replaces the old one (a profile name). Counters and sets need merge logic or a different data model.

challenges.learn:
Active-active writes: **Front Door** with latency routing sends pickers to their nearest region, and **Cosmos DB** with **multi-region writes** accepts writes locally in both. When two regions update the same item concurrently, the **conflict resolution policy** decides; for counters use a **custom** merge (or model stock as append-only movements).

The trade-offs: strong consistency isn't available with multiple write regions, multi-region writes cost more RUs, and every conflict-prone item needs thought.

challenges.title: Never charge twice
challenges.brief:
A food-ordering platform takes card payments through a payment provider. A payment must be charged exactly once, recorded, and announced to the kitchen and delivery services. Today the API charges the card, saves the payment, then publishes an event, and when it crashes between steps, customers are charged without an order or orders are cooked without a payment.

The payment path must also survive a zone failure.
functional: Charge the card for an order
Record the payment
Notify kitchen and delivery that the order is paid
nonFunctional: A retried request never charges twice
A payment is never saved without its event, or announced without being saved
Survives the loss of an availability zone
A struggling provider doesn't take down the API

numbers.label: Payments per minute at dinner peak (assume)

estimate.q: Without idempotency, how many timed-out calls a day could be retried into a double charge, if peak lasted all day?

tradeoff.q: Why not publish the "order paid" event straight from the API after saving?
choices: Saving and publishing are two systems; a crash in between loses or duplicates the event. The outbox commits both in one database transaction.
Service Bus can't receive messages from APIs.
Publishing directly is slower than polling.
tradeoff.why: The dual-write problem has no safe ordering. Writing to one system atomically and relaying from it removes the gap.

challenges.learn:
Exactly-once effects come from combining patterns. The payment API is **idempotent**: it stores an idempotency key with each charge and passes it to the provider. Calls to the provider use **timeouts, retries with jitter** and a **circuit breaker**. The payment row and an **outbox** row are written in one transaction to a **zone-redundant** database, and a relay publishes the outbox to **Service Bus** for kitchen and delivery.

The trade-off: events arrive slightly later (the relay's polling interval), and consumers must still be idempotent, because the relay can publish twice.

challenges.title: Scale on the backlog
challenges.brief: A document-conversion service receives jobs on a Service Bus queue. Jobs arrive in waves: nothing for hours, then 30,000 at once when a customer uploads an archive. Workers scale on CPU today, which reacts too slowly, and three idle workers run all night.

Converted files are stored
nonFunctional: Workers scale on the number of waiting jobs
No workers run when the queue is empty
A 30,000-job wave drains in about a minute

estimate.q: How many replicas drain the wave in a minute?
estimate.workings: 30,000 jobs ÷ 50 per replica per second = 600 replica-seconds ÷ 60 s = 10 replicas.

tradeoff.q: Why scale on queue length rather than CPU?
choices: Queue length measures the work waiting, so scaling starts before workers are overloaded and stops when the queue is empty.
CPU metrics aren't available for containers.
Queue-based scaling is always cheaper per replica.
tradeoff.why: CPU is a lagging signal and never reaches zero. The backlog says how much work is waiting right now.

challenges.learn:
Container Apps uses KEDA scalers: a **Service Bus scale rule** adds replicas as messages pile up and removes them as the queue drains, all the way to **zero**. Each replica is a **competing consumer** on the same queue.

The trade-offs: the first message after idle waits for a cold start, and the maximum replica count must stay within what downstream systems can absorb.

challenges.brief: A media company's platform team is moving twenty services onto Kubernetes. They want a production-grade first cluster: system components separated from app workloads, pods and nodes that scale with load, and no outage when a zone fails.

The cluster autoscaler replaces failed pods.
tradeoff.why: Pods need somewhere to run. Without node autoscaling, new pods stay pending; without pod autoscaling, new nodes sit empty.

A solid first **AKS** cluster: a **system node pool** for cluster components and a **user pool** for apps, the **horizontal pod autoscaler** and **cluster autoscaler** for elasticity, nodes spread across **availability zones**, at least two replicas per deployment, and the **Standard** tier for a financially backed control plane.

The trade-off: Kubernetes gives maximum control and portability, but upgrades, node images, networking and add-ons are now your team's job. Container Apps hides most of that.

challenges.title: Pull safely
challenges.brief:
A fintech's Container Apps pull their base images straight from a public registry at deploy time. Last month a public image was briefly replaced with a compromised one, and a deployment pulled it. Rate limits on the public registry also break deployments at busy times.

The security team wants every image to come from a private registry the company controls, pulled without passwords, over a private connection.

The CI pipeline pushes approved images
nonFunctional: Workloads only pull from the company's own registry
Pulls use identities, not registry passwords
The registry isn't reachable from the internet

choices: You control what's inside: images are scanned and pinned, and outages or tampering upstream don't reach production.
Public registries don't support HTTPS.
Private registries make images smaller.
tradeoff.why: Your registry becomes the gate: only what you imported and scanned can run.

challenges.learn:
Use **Azure Container Registry** as the only source of images: CI imports and scans base images, and apps pull with their **managed identity** (the AcrPull role), so there are no registry passwords. With the **Premium** tier, a **private endpoint** and public access off keep the registry off the internet.

The trade-off: Premium costs more, and the CI agents need a private path to the registry too.

challenges.title: Broker-agnostic
challenges.brief:
A logistics start-up's services publish and consume events. They use Service Bus in Azure but a different broker in their on-premises edition, and each service has broker-specific SDK code that the developers have to maintain twice.

They want services to publish and subscribe through one simple API, with the broker chosen by configuration.

The dispatch service subscribes to them
nonFunctional: Service code doesn't depend on a broker SDK
The broker can be swapped by configuration
Messaging uses Service Bus in Azure

tradeoff.q: What do you give up by using Dapr pub/sub instead of the Service Bus SDK directly?
choices: Some broker-specific features and a little latency through the sidecar, in exchange for portable, simpler service code.
Messages are no longer delivered reliably.
You can't use Service Bus anymore.
tradeoff.why: Abstractions cost access to the lowest common denominator. That's worth it when portability matters.

challenges.learn:
**Dapr** runs as a **sidecar** next to each container. Services publish with a plain HTTP call to the sidecar, and a Dapr pub/sub component, configured to use **Service Bus**, does the broker work. Swapping brokers means changing a component file, not code. Container Apps can enable Dapr with one setting.

The trade-off: the sidecar is another moving part, and broker-specific features (sessions, for example) may not map through the abstraction.

challenges.title: One door for APIs
challenges.brief:
A travel company split its monolith into five services: flights, hotels, cars, bookings and customers. Mobile apps now call five different hostnames, and every breaking change in a service breaks old app versions still in the stores.

They want one public API address, versioned, with the services hidden behind it.

Old app versions keep working on the old API version
nonFunctional: Services aren't reachable directly from the internet
API versions are managed in one place
Callers are rate-limited

choices: It becomes a critical shared component and a possible bottleneck; it must be redundant and its configuration carefully managed.
Gateways can only route to one service.
It forces all services to use the same database.
tradeoff.why: Gateway Routing simplifies clients and hides topology, at the price of a component that must never go down.

**API Management** gives clients one address and routes /flights, /hotels and so on to the right service (**Gateway Routing**). **Versioning** lets v1 and v2 live side by side while old apps age out, and **rate limits** protect the services. The services use internal ingress, so only the gateway can reach them.

The trade-off: the gateway is on every call. Give it a tier and redundancy that match its importance.

challenges.title: Own your data
challenges.brief:
An e-commerce team split its app into catalog, orders and customers services, but all three still read and write the same SQL database. A schema change by one team broke the other two last week, and the orders service can't scale its database without scaling everyone's.

Give each service its own data, and let services share information through APIs or events.

Orders still knows about products and customers
nonFunctional: No database is shared by two services
Each service owns its data store
Services exchange data through APIs or events, not tables

tradeoff.q: How does the orders service show a product name once catalog data is no longer in its database?
choices: It calls the catalog API, or keeps its own copy updated from catalog events.
It reads the catalog service's database directly.
It can't; orders must not show product names.
tradeoff.why: Owning data means others ask (API) or listen (events). Reading another service's tables brings the coupling back.

challenges.learn:
With **database per service**, each service owns its store and changes its schema freely; others get data through its API or by subscribing to its events. Stores can even differ: Cosmos DB for the catalog, SQL for orders.

The trade-offs: no more cross-service joins or transactions. You get eventual consistency between services, and patterns like sagas and the outbox to keep them in step.

challenges.title: Saga, orchestrated
challenges.brief:
A holiday booking takes five steps across services and partners: reserve the flight, reserve the hotel, charge the card, issue the tickets, send the confirmation. There's no distributed transaction across them. When the card charge fails, the flight and hotel stay reserved and nobody releases them.

The business wants every booking to end either fully completed or fully undone.
functional: Run the five booking steps in order
If a step fails, undo the steps already done
nonFunctional: Each booking ends fully completed or fully compensated
The workflow survives restarts mid-way
The flow is visible in one place

tradeoff.q: Orchestration or choreography for this saga?
choices: Orchestration: one coordinator knows the steps and compensations, which makes a five-step flow with partners easier to follow and change.
Choreography: it always needs fewer services.
Neither; use a distributed transaction across the partners.
tradeoff.why: Choreography (services reacting to events) suits short flows; as steps and compensations grow, a central orchestrator is easier to reason about.

challenges.learn:
A **saga** replaces one big transaction with a sequence of local ones plus **compensating** actions. A **Durable Functions** orchestrator calls each step in order, checkpoints after each, and on failure runs the compensations in reverse (cancel the hotel, cancel the flight).

The trade-offs: the system is temporarily inconsistent (a flight is held while payment runs), every step and compensation must be idempotent, and some actions, like an email already sent, can't really be undone.

challenges.title: Transactional outbox
challenges.brief:
An order service saves orders in Cosmos DB and then publishes an "order placed" message to Service Bus. Twice a week, the service crashes between the two, and either an order exists that the warehouse never hears about, or the warehouse ships an order that was never saved.

Make saving and publishing agree, always.

Publish an "order placed" message for each saved order
nonFunctional: Every saved order is published
Nothing is published that wasn't saved
Consumers handle the occasional duplicate

tradeoff.q: Why does the change feed solve the dual-write problem?
choices: The order write is the only write; the change feed reliably exposes it afterwards, so a relay can publish it even after crashes.
The change feed writes to Service Bus inside the same transaction.
It makes Cosmos DB writes faster.
tradeoff.why: Instead of writing to two systems, write once and derive the message from the durable change log. The relay retries until it succeeds.

challenges.learn:
The **Transactional Outbox**: the order service only writes the order to Cosmos DB. A function triggered by the **change feed** reads each new order and publishes it to Service Bus, and if it fails it retries from the same position. Saving and publishing can no longer disagree.

The trade-offs: publishing is slightly delayed, and the relay delivers at least once, so warehouse consumers must be idempotent.

challenges.brief:
A fleet-management app writes vehicle events to Cosmos DB. Managers' dashboards run heavy aggregate queries (distance per driver, fuel per depot) against the same container, burning RUs and throttling the event writes.

The writes must stay fast. Dashboards can be a few seconds behind.

Managers view aggregated dashboards and search
nonFunctional: Dashboard queries never touch the write store

numbers.label: Assume an aggregate query on the write store costs

estimate.q: How many RU/s do dashboard queries burn on the write store today?
estimate.workings: 300 queries/s × 400 RU = 120,000 RU/s, competing with the writes.

tradeoff.q: What do dashboards give up with a separate read model?
choices: Freshness: the view is updated from the change feed, so it lags the writes by a few seconds.
Accuracy: the numbers become estimates.
Security: anyone can read the view.
tradeoff.why: CQRS trades immediate consistency on the read side for independent scaling and cheap, simple reads.

challenges.learn:
**CQRS** separates writes from reads. The command side keeps writing events to Cosmos DB. A function on the **change feed** maintains a **materialized view** (pre-aggregated documents in a second container, or an AI Search index for search), and dashboards query only that view.

The trade-offs: two models to maintain, and the read side is eventually consistent. Rebuilding a view means replaying the change feed.

challenges.title: Work sign-in
challenges.brief:
A construction firm built an internal timesheet app on App Service with its own username and password table. Staff forget yet another password, and when people leave, nobody remembers to delete their accounts.

Employees already sign in to everything else with their work account and MFA.

nonFunctional: No separate passwords for this app

No authentication code to maintain in the app

tradeoff.q: Why use App Service's built-in authentication rather than an authentication library in the code?
choices: The platform handles redirects, token validation and sessions; the code just reads the signed-in user, so there's less to get wrong.
Libraries can't talk to Entra ID.
Built-in authentication works without an identity provider.
tradeoff.why: Easy Auth suits apps that just need sign-in. Use a library when you need fine-grained control over flows and tokens.

challenges.learn:
Use **Microsoft Entra ID** as the identity provider and turn on App Service **built-in authentication**: unauthenticated users are redirected to sign in with their work account (with MFA and Conditional Access), and the app receives their identity in headers. Disabling the work account removes access everywhere: **single sign-on** in both directions.

The trade-off: Easy Auth covers common scenarios; advanced flows (custom claims, multi-tenant logic) still need code.

challenges.title: Customers sign in
challenges.brief:
A meal-kit company is launching an app where customers sign up with email or their social accounts, manage subscriptions and see deliveries. The developers started building their own sign-up, password reset and social login code.

tradeoff.q: Why not put customers in the company's employee directory?
choices: Customer identity needs self-service sign-up, social logins and branding, and mixing customers with staff risks giving them access to internal apps.
The employee directory can't handle more than 1,000 accounts.
Customers can't use passwords.

**Microsoft Entra External ID** handles sign-up, sign-in, social identity providers, password reset and MFA for customers, in its own tenant separate from employees. The app obtains a token for the customer; the API (or API Management in front of it) **validates** that token on every call.

The trade-off: you depend on the identity service's flows and customization options, rather than owning every screen yourself.

A code review of a property-management app found the SQL connection string with a password, the storage account key and a mapping partner's API key sitting in app settings and, worse, in the Git history.

choices: With an identity there is no secret at all, so nothing to store, leak or rotate; Key Vault is for the secrets you can't eliminate.
Key Vault can't store connection strings.
Managed identities are faster than Key Vault lookups.
tradeoff.why: The best secret is one that doesn't exist. Vault the rest.

Turn on the app's **managed identity** and grant it roles on SQL and Storage, so those connections need **no secrets** at all. The partner's API key can't be eliminated, so store it in **Key Vault** and let the app read it with the same identity (Key Vault references in app settings do this without code changes).

The trade-off: role assignments become part of your deployment, and local development needs developer identities with similar roles.

challenges.title: Passwordless data
challenges.brief:
An order pipeline has an API that writes to Azure SQL and Blob Storage and sends to a Service Bus queue, and a worker function that reads the queue and writes to SQL. Every one of those connections uses a key or connection string, and the last key rotation broke production for an hour.

Make every connection into a data or messaging service passwordless.
functional: The API writes orders, files and messages
The worker reads messages and updates orders
nonFunctional: No connection into SQL, Storage or Service Bus uses a key or password
Every compute component has its own identity
Nothing to rotate

estimate.q: How many key rotations a year disappear?

tradeoff.q: After switching to managed identities, what else should you turn off?
choices: Local (key-based) authentication on the services, so a leaked old key can't be used anymore.
The services' encryption at rest.
HTTPS on the connections.
tradeoff.why: Passwordless isn't finished until the keys stop working. Many services can disable shared-key or SQL authentication.

challenges.learn:
Give the API and the worker **managed identities** and grant each the narrowest roles it needs (for example Storage Blob Data Contributor on one container, Service Bus Data Sender on one queue). Every connection then uses Entra ID tokens, so there is nothing to leak or rotate.

The trade-off: permissions move into role assignments that must be deployed and reviewed. Finish by disabling key-based authentication on the services.

challenges.title: Check the token
challenges.brief:
A logistics company exposes shipment APIs to its own apps and to partner systems. The backend services accept any request that reaches them, assuming "only our apps know the URL". A partner's script recently called an admin endpoint it was never meant to use.

Every call must carry a valid token from the company's identity platform, checked before it reaches a service.
functional: Apps and partners call shipment APIs with tokens
Services only see authenticated calls
nonFunctional: Calls without a valid token are rejected at the gateway
Services can't be reached around the gateway
Tokens come from Microsoft Entra ID

tradeoff.q: If the gateway validates tokens, should the backend services still check them?
choices: Ideally yes, at least the claims they rely on (Zero Trust); but the gateway check stops unauthenticated traffic early, before it costs anything.
No, backends must never see tokens.
Only if the gateway is down.
tradeoff.why: Gateway validation is the first line; services checking roles and claims for their own operations is defence in depth.

challenges.learn:
**API Management** with a **validate-jwt** policy checks each token's signature (against Entra ID's published keys), issuer, audience, expiry and roles before forwarding. Services use internal ingress, so the gateway is the only way in. This is **Zero Trust**: identity is verified on every call, not inferred from network location.

The trade-off: token lifetimes and app registrations become things to manage, and every client must be able to get tokens (for partners, the client-credentials flow).

challenges.title: Bring your own key
challenges.brief: A pension fund stores member records in Azure SQL and statements in Blob Storage. Its regulator now requires that data at rest is encrypted with keys the fund controls, can rotate, and can revoke in an emergency, and that the keys themselves can't be destroyed by an attacker or by accident.

Encrypt both with keys the fund controls
nonFunctional: SQL and Storage use customer-managed keys
Keys can't be permanently deleted during a retention period

tradeoff.q: What new risk do customer-managed keys bring?
choices: If the key is deleted or access to it is lost, the data becomes unreadable, which is why purge protection and access monitoring matter.
Data is no longer encrypted by Microsoft at all.
Customer-managed keys make every query slower by seconds.
tradeoff.why: Controlling the key also means owning its availability. Losing it is losing the data.

challenges.learn:
With **customer-managed keys**, SQL's TDE protector and Storage encryption use a key in your **Key Vault**. The services reach the vault with their **managed identities** to wrap and unwrap data keys. Turn on **soft delete** and **purge protection** so a deleted key can be recovered and can't be destroyed early.

The trade-off: you now own the key's lifecycle and availability. If the key is lost or access is broken, the data goes offline.

challenges.title: Layers of defence
challenges.brief:
A public ticket-resale API runs on VMs behind Application Gateway in one region. During a big on-sale it was hit by a volumetric flood, then by injection attempts, and an internal scan found the database still had a public endpoint.

Add the missing layers so that no single failed control exposes the data.
functional: Buyers and sellers call the public API
The API reads and writes listings in SQL
nonFunctional: Network floods against the public IP are mitigated
Web attacks are filtered before the API
The API subnet only accepts the traffic it needs
The database has no public endpoint

tradeoff.q: Why use both DDoS Protection and a WAF?
choices: They stop different attacks: DDoS Protection absorbs network floods; the WAF inspects HTTP requests for injection and other application attacks.
The WAF includes DDoS Protection, so one is enough.
DDoS Protection blocks SQL injection.
tradeoff.why: Layer 3/4 floods and layer 7 attacks need different tools. Defense in depth stacks them.

challenges.learn:
Each layer stops a different attack: **DDoS Network Protection** on the VNet absorbs floods against the public IP; the **Application Gateway WAF** blocks injection and other OWASP attacks; an **NSG** on the API subnet allows only gateway traffic; and a **private endpoint** with public access off keeps the database invisible.

The trade-off: DDoS Network Protection has a significant fixed monthly cost, worth it for internet-facing workloads where downtime is expensive.

choices: Defender detects threats in Azure resources; Sentinel collects those alerts plus logs from everywhere, correlates them into incidents and runs automated playbooks.

The trade-off: ingesting and retaining security logs costs money per GB, so choose sources and retention deliberately.

challenges.title: Landing zone
challenges.brief:
A bank is about to onboard twenty application teams to Azure. The platform team must provide the foundation before the first app lands: a governance hierarchy with guardrails, a central connectivity hub with a firewall for all egress, central logging, identity for everyone, and a standard way for apps to keep secrets.

tradeoff.q: Why separate platform subscriptions (connectivity, management) from application subscriptions?
choices: Different owners and permissions: the platform team controls shared networking and logging, and app teams can't change them by accident.
Azure requires one subscription per resource type.
It reduces the price of the firewall.
tradeoff.why: Subscriptions are access and billing boundaries. Separating platform from apps gives each team autonomy without risking shared infrastructure.

challenges.learn:
An **Azure landing zone**: a **management group** hierarchy with **Azure Policy** guardrails (deny or deploy-if-not-exists); a **connectivity** subscription with the hub VNet and **Azure Firewall**; a **management** subscription with the central **Log Analytics** workspace; **landing-zone** subscriptions where each app's spoke routes egress to the hub; **Entra ID** for every identity; and a **Key Vault** per app, reached with managed identities.

The trade-off: a lot of upfront platform work before the first app ships. It pays off from the second team onwards.

A food-delivery API has no monitoring beyond a CPU graph. Last Friday checkout returned errors for 40 minutes and the team found out from angry customers on social media.

challenges.brief:
Checkout in an outdoor-gear store sometimes takes eight seconds. A request passes through five services (web, cart, checkout, payment, shipping), each with its own logs, and every team says "it's not us".

The team wants to follow one slow request end to end and see which hop took the time.

choices: If one service drops the trace id, the timeline breaks there and the downstream spans can't be linked to the request.
Otherwise the services can't talk HTTP.
It's only needed for the first service.
tradeoff.why: Distributed tracing is a chain: one missing link and you're back to guessing.

challenges.learn:
Turn on **OpenTelemetry tracing** in every service and send it to one **Application Insights** resource. Each request carries a trace context (W3C traceparent) from service to service, so the end-to-end transaction view shows every span and which one took six of the eight seconds.

The trade-off: tracing every request is expensive at scale, so use sampling, ideally sampling whole traces rather than individual spans.

challenges.title: Find it
challenges.brief:
A hardware store's product search runs LIKE '%drill%' queries against the product database. It's slow, ignores typos and synonyms ("cordless" vs "battery"), can't filter by brand and price at the same time, and loads the database that checkout uses.

The product catalog lives in Cosmos DB and changes a few thousand times a day.

nonFunctional: Search doesn't query the operational database

Search keeps working if one search replica fails

tradeoff.q: Why an indexer instead of having the app push every change to the index?
choices: The indexer pulls changes from Cosmos DB on a schedule with change tracking built in, so the app has no extra write path to keep consistent.
Apps can't write to AI Search.
Indexers return search results faster.
tradeoff.why: Pull (indexer) is simpler; push gives fresher results. For thousands of changes a day, a few minutes' lag is fine.

challenges.learn:
**Azure AI Search** builds an inverted index with analyzers (stemming, synonyms, typo tolerance) and supports facets and filters, all far beyond what LIKE queries can do. An **indexer** pulls changes from Cosmos DB on a schedule, so the index follows the catalog without app changes.

The trade-offs: the index is eventually consistent with the database, and search units cost money: use at least two replicas for query availability and add partitions as the index grows.

challenges.title: Live numbers
challenges.brief:
A grocery chain's operations room wants a wall screen showing orders per minute for every region, updated live, with history to compare against last week. Order events already flow from the checkout systems.

The nightly report is useless for spotting a payment outage in one region at 18:05.

tradeoff.q: Which window fits "orders per minute"?
choices: Tumbling: fixed, non-overlapping one-minute windows, so each order is counted exactly once.
Session: windows that close after inactivity.
Sliding: a new window for every event.
tradeoff.why: Tumbling windows map directly to "per minute". Hopping or sliding windows suit moving averages.

challenges.learn:
Order events land in **Event Hubs**. A **Stream Analytics** job counts them per region over **tumbling one-minute windows** and writes the results to **Data Explorer**, which also keeps history for fast KQL comparisons. **Managed Grafana** reads Data Explorer for the wall screen.

The trade-offs: windows emit when they close, so numbers lag up to a window, and late events need a tolerance policy.

choices: Optimistic for most rooms (rare conflicts, no locks held); a conflict means "sorry, just taken". Pessimistic locks suit very hot inventory where retries would pile up.

After commit, a **Service Bus** message drives confirmation emails and the sync to hotel systems.

The trade-off: search availability is slightly stale, so the booking step must always re-check against the database.

choices: More copies of everything to deploy, monitor and pay for, plus a tenant catalog and routing layer to maintain.
Tenants can no longer have their own data.

tradeoff.why: Stamps buy isolation and scale-out with operational overhead. Automation (infrastructure as code, safe deployment rings) is essential.

challenges.learn:
With **Deployment Stamps**, each stamp is a complete copy of the stack (app plus its own database) serving a few hundred tenants. A **tenant catalog** records which stamp each tenant lives on, and **Front Door** routes by tenant hostname to the right stamp. Stamps in different regions satisfy data residency, and deployments roll out stamp by stamp.

The trade-offs: more infrastructure to automate and pay for, and cross-tenant features (global search, reporting) need their own design.

challenges.title: Modernize the monolith
challenges.brief:
A distributor runs a 15-year-old .NET Framework order system on two Windows VMs, with a SQL Server database that uses SQL Agent jobs and cross-database queries. A big-bang rewrite failed once already.

The new plan: move the database to a managed service with minimal changes, put a router in front, and carve out the orders module as a new service first, while everything else keeps running on the old system.
functional: Users keep using the same URL
/orders goes to the new service; everything else goes to the monolith
Both read the migrated database
nonFunctional: The database runs on a managed service with SQL Server compatibility
Features move one at a time with no big-bang cut-over
Rollback is a routing change

estimate.q: How many quarters until every module has moved?
estimate.workings: 14 modules ÷ 2 per quarter = 7 quarters (under two years).

tradeoff.q: Why SQL Managed Instance rather than Azure SQL Database for this database?
choices: It keeps instance-level features the app relies on (SQL Agent, cross-database queries), so the database moves with minimal changes.
SQL Database can't store more than 1 GB.
Managed Instance doesn't need a network.
tradeoff.why: Pick the target that minimises changes during migration; optimise later.

challenges.learn:
The **Strangler Fig** pattern: **Application Gateway** with **path-based routing** sends /orders to a new **App Service** app and everything else to the monolith VMs. Each quarter another module moves, and rollback is a routing change. The database moves first to **SQL Managed Instance** for near-full SQL Server compatibility.

The trade-off: for a while you run two systems against a shared database, which couples them. Plan to give carved-out services their own data over time.

challenges.title: Food delivery, worldwide
challenges.brief:
The final design: a food-delivery platform serving customers on three continents. It must be fast everywhere, keep taking orders when an availability zone or a whole region fails, keep every data store off the internet, use no passwords or keys between services, and let engineers trace any order end to end.

And it must fit the budget.
functional: Customers browse restaurants and place orders
Orders are processed and tracked
Customers sign in with their own accounts
nonFunctional: Served from three regions behind one global entry point with a WAF
Every tier survives a zone failure; the platform survives a region failure
No data store has a public endpoint
Every connection into data is passwordless
Every service is traced
Total cost at most 50 units

estimate.q: Orders per second at peak?

tradeoff.q: Which pillar usually gives way when you add regions, zones and private networking?
choices: Cost: every region and zone adds capacity, and private networking and premium tiers add fixed charges, so you trade money for reliability and security.
Security: private endpoints make the design less secure.
Performance: more regions always make it slower.
tradeoff.why: The Well-Architected pillars pull against each other. Good designs make the trade-offs deliberately, and the budget forces you to choose.

challenges.learn:
A **geode** design: **Front Door Premium** with a managed **WAF** and Private Link origins routes each customer to the nearest of three regions. Each region runs **zone-redundant** Container Apps, all on **Cosmos DB** replicated to the same three regions. Data has **private endpoints** only, every connection uses **managed identities**, and all services send traces to **Application Insights**.

This is the **Well-Architected** balance in one picture: each pillar's gains cost something on another, and the budget makes you choose what is enough.
